scene.note: Each query asks a small question inside a bigger one, so the numbers it compares against are worked out fresh every time it runs.

steps.note: Every product comes in. A loaf and a croissant are not compared with each other, only with their own category.
For each product, a small query inside works out the average price of that product's category.
The inner query reads the category from the outer row, so it gives a different average for bread than for pastry.
A product stays when its price is above its own category's average. No number is typed in, so a new price list still works.

value.label: the shape of what comes back

steps.note: Tobias gets the dear products, by category from A to Z and dearest first within each.
The query looks at one cafe at a time.

value.label: one order of this cafe, with its items

steps.note: For that cafe, the inner query walks from its orders to their items and on to each product's category.
Order 31 has a cake, but it was cancelled, so it does not count. Only a delivered order with a cake product does.
The inner query only has to answer yes or no. One matching order is enough, so a cafe that bought ten cakes still appears once.

value.label: the shape of what comes back

steps.note: Tobias gets each cafe that buys cake once, in any order.
Each line of a delivered order is worth its quantity times the product's current price.

value.label: the first step, named with WITH

steps.note: The first step adds the lines up per cafe and gives that small table a name. Cafes with no delivered order are not in it.
The average spend is worked out from that named table, over the cafes in it.
Each cafe's total is compared with the average before any rounding, then the cafe's name is joined in.

value.label: the shape of what comes back

steps.note: Odile gets the cafes that spend above average, highest spend first.
